name: Static stretching

card.summary: Holding a muscle in a lengthened position to build flexibility and range of motion, which supports better posture, training and movement.
card.note: Long holds immediately before maximal effort can temporarily reduce strength and power.

quick.overview:
Static stretching means moving a joint to the end of its range and holding the position. It is the classic form of stretching and is used to increase flexibility and range of motion.

Better mobility helps people reach positions in training, sit and stand with better posture, and move more smoothly, all of which feed into how someone carries and presents their body.
quick.how: Stretches are typically held for a period for each muscle group, often after training or as a separate mobility session. Many people place them after workouts rather than before and use dynamic warm-ups beforehand.
quick.risks: Stretching is generally low-risk. Reviews report that very long holds before maximal efforts can modestly reduce performance for a short time, and overstretching can strain tissue.

lead: Static stretching means moving a joint to the end of its range and holding the position, and it is the simplest and most familiar form of flexibility work.[4] People use it to increase range of motion, ease stiffness, reach deeper positions in training and recover after exercise, and in appearance-focused circles it is paired with posture and mobility routines for hips, hamstrings, chest and shoulders.

For looks, the payoff runs through movement and training. More range of motion lets lifters train through fuller ranges, and flexible hips, hamstrings and chest are part of how many people set up their stance and gait. A 2016 meta-analysis of 19 trials in healthy young adults found that static stretching increased hamstring flexibility on all three tests used.[8] A 2023 meta-analysis found a moderate decrease in muscle stiffness after 3 to 12 weeks of static stretch training.[2]

Research also covers questions that matter to people who stretch for training reasons. A 2024 meta-analysis of 42 randomised trials found small gains in maximal strength and muscle size from chronic static stretching,[5] while a second 2024 meta-analysis of 23 trials in healthy people found that stretching alone did not change spinal or pelvic posture, whereas strengthening did.[6] A 2016 review found that long holds immediately before maximal efforts reduce performance a little, and shorter holds do so less.[3][9]

chain: Hold muscles in lengthened positions regularly
Greater range of motion and lower muscle stiffness
Easier good posture and fuller movement in training
angle.text: Static stretching increases how far joints move, which people use to improve posture and training positions. Gains in flexibility are one input to how upright and fluid someone looks.

paras: Wikipedia defines stretching as a form of exercise in which a muscle or tendon is deliberately extended to improve its felt elasticity, muscle tone, flexibility and range of motion. Static stretches are held while stationary; the simplest form is static-passive, in which an external force such as a partner, a wall or the other limb takes the joint to its end of range. A more advanced variant, proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF), combines contractions with external force.[4]

Dynamic stretching, by contrast, moves a joint through its range, as in lunges, and ballistic stretching uses bouncing or swinging.[4] Wikipedia notes that static and PNF stretching are more effective for flexibility than dynamic or ballistic stretching, and that strength training can also increase range of motion.[4]

sections.h: How stretching changes range of motion
paras: Researchers describe two main explanations. A sensory theory holds that people get better at tolerating the stretch sensation, while a mechanical theory holds that tissue stiffness or muscle geometry changes. Wikipedia says the roles of the two are not well understood.[4] Titin, a protein in muscle fibres, contributes to passive tension.[4]

The 2023 meta-analysis by Takeuchi and colleagues pooled 10 studies of static stretch training lasting at least two weeks. It found a moderate decrease in muscle stiffness after 3 to 12 weeks (effect size -0.749), with no significant difference by sex and no significant relationship between total stretching time and stiffness. An earlier meta-analysis had reported no stiffness change, and the authors noted that more studies had appeared since.[2]

Flexibility work is used to reach positions in training, such as deep squats, overhead presses and hip hinge patterns, and to relieve stiffness in the hips, hamstrings, calves and chest. A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 randomised and controlled trials in healthy young adults found that static stretching beat control conditions on the passive straight-leg raise, passive knee extension and active knee extension tests.[8]

Stretching tight muscles and strengthening their opposing muscles is a common approach to posture changes such as rounded shoulders or an anterior pelvic tilt. A 2024 systematic review with meta-analysis by Warneke, Lohmann and Wilke pooled 23 controlled trials with 969 healthy participants. It found no change in spinal or lumbopelvic posture from acute stretching (d = 0.01) or chronic stretching (d = -0.19), while chronic strengthening produced large improvements (d = -0.83) and was superior to stretching. Strengthening worked in the thoracic and cervical spine but not in the lumbar and lumbopelvic region. The authors concluded that moderate-certainty evidence does not support stretching as a treatment for muscle imbalance and recommended focusing on strengthening.[6] Posture-minded lifters often combine held stretches with strength work.[6]

A 2024 meta-analysis by Warneke and colleagues examined chronic static stretching in 42 randomised controlled trials with 1,318 participants. It found a small increase in maximal strength (d = 0.30) and a small hypertrophy effect (d = 0.20). Longer stretching durations, longer programs and higher frequencies produced small but significant effects, and lower doses did not reach significance. The authors concluded that chronic static stretching has a minor effect but may be a possible alternative to resistance training, and that a dose-response relationship warrants further study.[5] Wikipedia notes that long-term stretching may slightly increase strength, with a larger effect in sedentary people.[4]

Static stretching before exercise has been studied for effects on power and speed. A 2016 systematic review by Behm, Blazevich, Kay and McHugh reported performance changes of -3.7% for static stretching, +1.3% for dynamic stretching and -4.4% for PNF when tested immediately after stretching. Holds of 60 seconds or more per muscle group were associated with larger deficits (-4.6%) than holds under 60 seconds (-1.1%), and stretching at longer muscle lengths showed a small benefit (2.2%). When dynamic activity followed the stretching, the review found no clear performance effect, and it recommended stretching within a warm-up that includes post-stretch dynamic activity.[9]

A 2011 review by Behm and Chaouachi noted many studies showing stretch-induced impairments and a growing number showing none, and suggested the lack of impairment may relate to factors such as short duration (under 90 seconds total) and an intensity below the point of discomfort.[3] Wikipedia advises an active dynamic warm-up before exercise for these reasons.[4]

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 randomised trials (229 participants) compared post-exercise stretching with passive recovery. It found no effect on strength recovery or on delayed-onset muscle soreness at 24, 48 and 72 hours, rated confidence in the evidence as very low, and noted that about 70% of studies had a high risk of bias.[1] Wikipedia likewise says it found no evidence that stretching reduces soreness, though it may give psychological comfort.[4]

A 2022 evidence-based review of exercise-associated muscle cramps reports that treatment of acute cramps continues to include gentle static stretching until symptoms ease.[7] On injury, the 2016 review found no clear effect of static or PNF stretching on all-cause or overuse injuries,[9] and Wikipedia notes that dynamic warm-ups reduce injury risk in several team sports and that static stretching may lower muscle injury risk while possibly raising bone and joint injury risk.[4]

Wikipedia states that incorrect stretching can cause hypermobility, instability or permanent damage to tendons, ligaments and muscle fibres, and that ballistic stretching may damage joints.[4] Reviews report that very long holds before maximal efforts can temporarily reduce force and power.[3][9]

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised trials have examined static stretching's effect on hamstring flexibility,[8] muscle stiffness,[2] strength and muscle size,[5] posture,[6] acute performance,[3][9] and post-exercise recovery.[1] Reviews of acute stretching report no clear effect on all-cause or overuse injuries.[9]

timeline.event: Behm and Chaouachi review the acute effects of static and dynamic stretching on performance.[3]
Meta-analysis finds static stretching increases hamstring flexibility in 19 trials; Behm and colleagues publish a systematic review of acute stretching effects.[8][9]
Meta-analysis of post-exercise stretching finds no effect on strength recovery or soreness versus passive recovery.[1]
Meta-analysis reports a moderate decrease in muscle stiffness after 3-12 weeks of static stretch training.[2]
Meta-analyses report small strength and size gains from chronic static stretching and no posture change from stretching alone.[5][6]

lore.intro: In fitness and posture-focused communities static stretching is discussed as a way to fix tightness, improve posture and reach deeper training positions, and as something to do or avoid before lifting.

claims.claim: Stretching tight muscles fixes posture problems such as rounded shoulders or anterior pelvic tilt
claims.believers: Posture routines commonly pair stretching of tight muscles with strengthening of their opposing muscles, on the idea of correcting a muscle imbalance.[6]
claims.experts: A 2024 meta-analysis of 23 trials found no posture change from acute or chronic stretching in healthy people, while strengthening produced large improvements.[6]

claims.claim: Static stretching before lifting hurts performance
claims.believers: Lifters and coaches commonly prefer dynamic warm-ups and keep long holds for after training.[4]
claims.experts: Reviews report small immediate declines after static stretching, larger with holds of 60 seconds or more and absent or reduced with short holds or when dynamic activity follows.[3][9]

claims.believers: Many exercisers stretch during cool-downs to ease soreness and speed recovery.[1]
claims.experts: A 2021 meta-analysis of 10 trials found no effect on soreness or strength recovery versus passive rest, with very low confidence in the evidence.[1]

claims.claim: Stretching increases flexibility and range of motion
claims.believers: Practitioners report being able to reach deeper positions after regular stretching.[4]
claims.experts: A 2016 meta-analysis of 19 trials found static stretching increased hamstring flexibility in healthy young adults; reviews report range-of-motion gains from all stretching types.[8][9]

claims.claim: Long stretching sessions can build muscle
claims.believers: Some lifters stretch for long durations hoping to add muscle size.[5]
claims.experts: A 2024 meta-analysis of 42 trials found small gains in strength (d = 0.30) and size (d = 0.20), larger with longer durations and frequencies.[5]

claims.believers: Stretching is widely recommended in warm-ups to avoid injury.[4]
claims.experts: A 2016 review found no clear effect of static or PNF stretching on all-cause or overuse injuries; dynamic warm-ups reduce injury in some sports.[4][9]
